title: Routing Information Protocol
summary: Describes the Routing Information Protocol, an existing way for gateways and hosts to exchange routing information, written as a basis for gateway software. It is a distance-vector protocol widely used in practice. It is historic, and later updated by RFC 1388 and RFC 1723.

plainLanguage.summary: Neighbors tell each other how many steps away every place is, and each keeps the shortest route it hears. RIP was one of the first written-down systems for sharing routes between networks, and this document set out its rules.

questions: how does the routing information protocol work
why is rip limited to 15 hops
subtitle: How early gateways swapped distance tables so every router could find the shortest path.

tldr.problem: Gateways and hosts on an IP network need to learn which neighbor to send each datagram to, but the widely used routing program routed had never been formally documented and implementations disagreed in details.
tldr.mechanism: Each participant periodically tells its neighbors the distance (metric) to every destination it knows. Receivers add the cost of the network the update arrived on and keep the smallest total, using split horizon and triggered updates to limit routing loops.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is marked Historic and was later updated by RFC 1388 and RFC 1723. It is limited to networks whose longest path is 15 hops and relies on counting to infinity to resolve some loops.

today: RFC 1058 is marked Historic and was later updated by RFC 1388 and RFC 1723. It is the original written description of RIP version 1.

sections.title: What RIP Is and What It Is Not
sections.content:
The Routing Information Protocol (RIP) documents an existing protocol for exchanging routing information among gateways and other hosts, based on the program routed shipped with the 4.3 Berkeley Software Distribution. Several other implementations claimed to be the same protocol but disagreed in details, so this document combines features from various implementations. The author expects a program built from it to interoperate with routed and the other implementations he knows of.

RIP is intended as an interior gateway protocol (IGP) inside one autonomous system, for moderate-size networks of reasonably homogeneous technology. The RFC lists three specific limits: the protocol is limited to networks whose longest path involves 15 hops, it depends on counting to infinity to resolve certain unusual loops, and its fixed metrics cannot choose routes by measured delay, reliability or load.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP is a way for the routers of one network to share a map of roads. It suits medium-sized networks of similar equipment, not large or complicated ones.

sections.title: Distance Vector Routing and Its Safeguards
sections.content:
RIP belongs to the class of distance vector algorithms. Every participant keeps a routing database with, for each destination, the next gateway and a metric measuring the total distance. It periodically sends its neighbors the contents of that database. When an update arrives from a neighbor G', the receiver adds the cost of the network the update came over to get a new distance. It adopts the new route if the distance is smaller than the one it has, or if the update comes from the gateway the current route already uses, even when the new metric is larger.

A gateway that crashes cannot announce the fact, so routes must time out. RIP sends updates every 30 seconds and treats a route as invalid after 180 seconds without a word. An unreachable network is advertised with the metric 16, which acts as infinity. The RFC explains that infinity is kept as small as possible: when a network becomes unreachable, metrics can creep upward in a loop called counting to infinity, and a small infinity ends that sooner.

Two defenses are specified. Split horizon avoids claiming reachability for a destination to the neighbor the route was learned from, either by leaving the route out (simple split horizon) or by advertising it with metric 16 (split horizon with poisoned reverse). Triggered updates make a gateway send changed metrics almost immediately instead of waiting for the next regular update. Neither fully prevents counting to infinity.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router tells its neighbors how far away each place is, and keeps the smallest distance it hears. A router never tells a neighbor about a road that runs back through that same neighbor, and it announces a broken road at once instead of waiting its turn.

sections.title: RIP Messages
sections.content:
RIP runs on top of UDP. Each host's routing process sends and receives datagrams on UDP port 520. Unsolicited updates use port 520 for both source and destination; replies to a request go back to the port the request came from. A silent process never sends messages but still listens, which suits hosts that are not gateways.

Every datagram has a command, a version (this document describes version 1) and a list of route entries. Each entry holds an address family identifier (2 means IP), an IP address, and a metric. The metric is a value from 1 to 15, or 16 for an unreachable destination. The entry portion may appear up to 25 times in one datagram, and the maximum datagram size is 512 octets, counting only the RIP fields and not the IP or UDP headers. A large routing table is simply split across several datagrams.

The commands are request (1) and response (2). Commands 3 (traceon) and 4 (traceoff) are obsolete and their messages are ignored; 5 is reserved for Sun Microsystems. Datagrams with version zero are ignored, and for version 1 any field marked "must be zero" that is nonzero makes the whole message be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A RIP message is a short form carrying a list of lines. Each line says which place is meant and how many steps away it is. Every router sends and listens on a fixed mailbox number, 520.

sections.title: Addresses, Subnets and Default Routes
sections.content:
RIP messages do not distinguish types of address. A field labeled "address" can hold a host address, a subnet number, a network number, or 0.0.0.0 for a default route. When routing a datagram, a host uses the most specific match available: it checks host addresses first, then subnet or network numbers, and finally falls back to the default route.

Because hosts normally know subnet masks only for directly connected networks, a border gateway must not send subnet routes outside the network the subnet belongs to. It sends a single entry for the whole network instead, and host routes subsumed by a network route are hidden. The special address 0.0.0.0 describes a default route and is handled like an ordinary network entry. Support for it is not required but is strongly recommended; implementations that do not support it must ignore such entries and must not pass them on.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can talk about one computer, one subnet, a whole network, or everywhere else. They always use the most exact match they have, and they keep subnet details inside their own network.

sections.title: Timers and Processing
sections.content:
Every 30 seconds the output process generates a complete response for every neighboring gateway. To stop gateways from synchronizing their updates, implementations must either drive the timer from a clock unaffected by system load or add a small random time each time the timer is set.

Each route has a timeout and a garbage-collection timer. The timeout restarts whenever an update for the route arrives; if 180 seconds pass, the route is no longer valid. The deletion process sets the metric to 16, starts a 120-second garbage-collection timer, and signals a triggered response. Until that timer expires the route is still advertised, with metric 16; then it is removed.

On input, responses are only accepted from port 520 and from a neighbor on a directly connected network, and a host ignores copies of its own broadcasts. For each entry the receiver computes metric = MIN (metric + cost, 16), and a route with an infinite metric is never added as a new route. A request for the whole table is answered using normal output processing, including split horizon and subnet hiding, while a request for specific destinations is answered with exact metrics and no filtering because it is meant for diagnostics. Triggered updates are rate limited: after one is sent, a timer is set for a random time between 1 and 5 seconds, and changes during that window are combined into a single update.
sections.plainLanguage: Every half minute each router reads out its whole list to its neighbors. If a route goes quiet for three minutes, the router declares it unreachable, tells everyone, and only later forgets it.

sections.title: Optional Control Functions
sections.content:
The last section describes administrative controls that are not part of the protocol itself but which the RFC strongly recommends including. They exist because hosts are sometimes misconfigured and begin sending inappropriate information, and because a site may not want other organizations to reach a network it uses only for its own traffic.

Typical controls are a neighbor list, so that a host accepts response messages only from listed neighbors, and lists of destination addresses to allow or disallow, tied to a particular interface and to the incoming or outgoing direction. If an allow list is given, all other addresses are disallowed; if a disallow list is given, all other addresses are allowed. The RFC stresses that the protocol does not require these or any other controls.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can keep a list of neighbors it trusts and a list of places it may mention, so that one confused machine cannot spoil everyone's map.

fields.desc: 1 to 15 for a route, or 16 for unreachable.
